A1-A2.headline: How Alexander Fleming Discovered Penicillin By Accident

pages.text:
The story of Penicillin is one of the greatest wins in modern health care. Long before science labs, early people saw that some plants helped bad cuts get well.

Even so, they never knew the exact active part.
pages.caption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin.

imageProvenance.credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/12/d4/a9331961bf9ec04b09fa2f7fffb8.jpg archive Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0059573.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-29): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/xkbnmutd C

evidence.fileTitle: File:Glass phial of British Standard penicillin, London, England, Wellcome L0059573.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin

pages.text:
A big turning point came in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital in London. Scottish doctor Alexander Fleming left his glass test plates behind for a summer break.

When he came back, a tiny green spot had cleared a wide ring.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his London laboratory.

evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1943
evidence.articleSection: Discovery of the properties of mould juice

pages.text:
Fleming saw that the liquid from that green spot could fight illness. Still, he lacked the lab tools to make it clean and pure.

In 1939, an Oxford University team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain grew it safely.
pages.caption: Howard Florey during his research work.

imageProvenance.credit: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin Past, Present and Future- the Development and Production of Penicillin, England, 1944 D17803.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Howard Florey in his office in 1944

pages.text:
Turning a lab find into real medicine took huge factory work. During World War II, American and British teams learned how to grow it in big tanks.

Soon, full supplies reached Allied soldiers and saved many lives.
pages.caption: Glass vessels used to grow penicillin mould.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in laboratories to produce penicillin. The mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with nutrients. The stopper kept contaminants out while allowing the mould to get fresh air.

pages.text:
For their great work, Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Their work changed health care across the whole world.

Wide access to Penicillin helped cure once-deadly illnesses and showed how shared science can keep people safe everywhere.

B1-B2.headline: The Remarkable Story Behind the Discovery of Penicillin

pages.text:
The discovery of penicillin stands among the greatest wins in modern medicine. Long before science labs existed, ancient healers noticed certain molds helped bad cuts heal.

Yet they could never isolate the active substance.
pages.caption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin.

imageProvenance.credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/12/d4/a9331961bf9ec04b09fa2f7fffb8.jpg archive Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0059573.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-29): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/xkbnmutd C

pages.text:
A major turning point came in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital in London. Scottish doctor Alexander Fleming left bacterial plates behind during a summer break.

On returning, he saw a clear ring around a stray mold where germs failed to grow.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his London laboratory.

evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1943
evidence.articleSection: Discovery of the properties of mould juice

pages.text:
Although Fleming saw the germ-fighting power of the mold juice, he lacked the tools to make it pure.

In 1939, an Oxford team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain extracted the drug and proved its safety in animal tests.
pages.caption: Howard Florey during his research work.

pages.text:
Turning a lab find into daily medicine took huge factory effort. During World War II, American and British teams built mass production using giant tanks.

Full supplies soon reached Allied soldiers and saved countless lives.
pages.caption: Glass vessels used to grow penicillin mould.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in laboratories to produce penicillin. The mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with nutrients. The stopper kept contaminants out while allowing the mould to get fresh air.

pages.text:
In honor of their landmark work, Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Wide access to penicillin reshaped global health care. It proved that shared scientific research could beat once-deadly bacterial illnesses.

C1-C2.headline: From Serendipitous Observation to Therapeutic Paradigm

pages.text:
Penicillin's emergence marks a transformative milestone in modern medicine. Long before laboratories, ancient healers observed curative traits in molds and plants.

Yet early practitioners never isolated the bioactive agent.
pages.caption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin.

imageProvenance.credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/12/d4/a9331961bf9ec04b09fa2f7fffb8.jpg archive Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0059573.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-29): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/xkbnmutd C

evidence.fileTitle: File:Glass phial of British Standard penicillin, London, England, Wellcome L0059573.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin

pages.text:
A pivotal juncture unfolded in 1928 at London's St Mary's Hospital. While Scottish physician Alexander Fleming vacationed, an airborne mold spore colonized his dish.

Returning, he discovered a sterile halo around the growth.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his London laboratory.

evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1943
evidence.articleSection: Discovery of the properties of mould juice

pages.text:
Although Fleming discerned the broth's antibacterial potency, he lacked biochemical means to purify it.

In 1939, Oxford scientists Howard Florey and Ernst Chain isolated the compound and confirmed its safety in animals.
pages.caption: Howard Florey during his research work.

imageProvenance.credit: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin Past, Present and Future- the Development and Production of Penicillin, England, 1944 D17803.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Howard Florey in his office in 1944

pages.text:
Translating a laboratory anomaly into clinical therapy demanded immense industrial mobilization. During World War II, Anglo-American teams built huge fermentation tanks.

Mass production equipped Allied troops, saving lives.
pages.caption: Glass vessels used to grow penicillin mould.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in laboratories to produce penicillin. The mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with nutrients. The stopper kept contaminants out while allowing the mould to get fresh air.

pages.text:
Recognizing these monumental achievements, Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain jointly received the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Widespread penicillin availability revolutionized global therapeutics, demonstrating how collaborative empirical research could vanquish formerly incurable bacterial infections.
